text: The 2012 Delhi gang rape and murder, known as the Nirbhaya case, occurred on 16 December 2012 in Munirka, Delhi, when 22-year-old Jyoti Singh, a physiotherapy intern, was gang-raped and tortured in a private bus while travelling with her friend, Awindra Pratap Pandey. The bus, which had only six passengers including the driver, deviated from its route and its doors were shut, prompting suspicion from Pandey, who was then taunted by the group. A scuffle followed, during which Pandey was beaten, gagged, and knocked unconscious with an iron rod, and Jyoti was dragged to the rear of the bus, where she was raped and severely injured with a blunt object—later identified as a rusted, L-shaped wheel jack handle—causing extensive damage to her abdomen, intestines, and genitals. Jyoti attempted to fight back, biting three of the attackers. After the assault, both victims were thrown from the moving bus; one of the perpetrators cleaned the vehicle, which was later impounded. The partially clothed victims were found by a passerby around 11 pm and taken to Safdarjung Hospital, where Jyoti received emergency treatment and was placed on mechanical ventilation. She had numerous bite marks and injuries, and medical staff confirmed penetration by a metal rod. On 27 December, she was flown to Mount Elizabeth Hospital in Singapore for further treatment, where she suffered a cardiac arrest during a six-hour flight and died at 4:45 am on 29 December (2:15 am IST). Her body was cremated on 30 December in Delhi under high police security. The incident sparked widespread national and international outrage, leading to public protests in New Delhi and major cities across India, demanding better women's safety and security. Six men were arrested: Ram Singh, the driver, and his brother Mukesh Singh, both from Ravidas camp; Vinay Sharma, a 26-year-old assistant gym instructor; Pawan Gupta, a 19-year-old fruit seller; Akshay Thakur, a 28-year-old man seeking employment; and the juvenile Mohammed Afroz, 17 years and six months old, from Badayun. The juvenile was convicted under the Juvenile Justice Act and sentenced to three years in a reform facility. The adult defendants—Pawan Gupta, Vinay Sharma, Akshay Thakur, and Mukesh Singh—were found guilty of rape and murder on 10 September 2013 and sentenced to death; the Delhi High Court upheld the verdict on 13 March 2014, and the Supreme Court rejected their final appeals on 18 December 2019. The four adult convicts were executed by hanging on 20 March 2020. Ram Singh died in police custody on 11 March 2013, with authorities stating it was unclear whether it was suicide or murder. The case led to the formation of a judicial committee that reviewed 80,000 public suggestions and concluded that government and police failures were the root cause of crimes against women. In 2013, the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act was passed by President Pranab Mukherjee, introducing new laws and creating six fast-track courts for rape cases. Despite these reforms, critics argue the legal system remains slow, though public discourse on women's safety has significantly increased. The victim's father initially opposed revealing her name, but later stated that he wanted the world to know her real name, Jyoti Singh, to honor her courage and inspire other survivors. In compliance with Indian law, her name was not publicly released initially, and media used pseudonyms such as Nirbhaya, meaning "fearless," Damini, or Delhi braveheart. The Delhi police registered a case against the editor of Mail Today for disclosing her identity under section 228(A) of the Indian Penal Code. A Special Investigation Team, led by Pramod Kumar Kushwaha, was formed to probe the case. The attackers had previously robbed a carpenter, Ramadhir Singh, who reported the incident to three police constables from Hauz Khas, who refused to act, citing jurisdictional issues. The Delhi High Court reprimanded the police for being evasive in their probe status report, and two Assistant Commissioners were suspended for failing to prevent the incident. The government appointed a medical committee on 21 December to ensure Jyoti received optimal care, and on 26 December, a cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh decided to transfer her to Singapore, a decision criticized by some doctors as politically motivated. The juvenile defendant, later renamed Raju in media, was arrested at Anand Vihar terminal and had only met the others that day. The case led to significant changes in public awareness and policy, though the victim's father later expressed regret that justice had not been fully achieved.

The Delhi High Court approved the establishment of five fast-track courts to handle rape and sexual assault cases. The first of these courts was inaugurated on 2 January 2013 by Altamas Kabir, Chief Justice of India, at the Saket court complex in South Delhi. On 21 December 2012, the Delhi High Court criticized the Delhi police for being "evasive" in a probe status report detailing officers on patrol duty in an area covered by a bus route, with a further hearing scheduled for 9 January 2013. The next day, the Delhi Police took action against three Hauz Khas police station personnel for inaction in responding to a robbery that occurred on the same bus. On 24 December, two Assistant Commissioners of Police were suspended for failing to prevent a gang rape incident. The juvenile defendant Mohammed Afroz, later referred to as Raju in the media due to his age, was declared 17 years and six months old on the day of the crime by the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB), based on his birth certificate and school documents, and the JJB rejected a police request for a bone ossification test to verify his age. On 28 January 2013, the JJB ruled that Afroz would not be tried as an adult, rejecting a petition by Janata Party president Subramanian Swamy to prosecute him as an adult due to the violent nature of the alleged crime. The minor was tried separately in a juvenile court. The verdict was initially scheduled for 25 July 2013, deferred to 5 August, and then to 19 August; on 31 August, he was convicted of rape and murder under the Juvenile Justice Act and sentenced to three years' imprisonment in a reform facility, including the eight months he spent in remand. Reportedly, Jyoti's younger brother attempted to attack the juvenile after the verdict but was restrained by the crowd. Afroz was released on 20 December 2015. To support his rehabilitation and mainstreaming as required by the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000, management committees were established before his release, and a 'post-release plan' was submitted to the Delhi High Court in December 2015. The plan, prepared by a committee headed by an officer from the District Child Protection Unit, recommended that Afroz should lead a new life with a new identity if permissible to avoid backlash, and noted that he had learned cooking and tailoring during his stay in the reform house. The report recommended a one-time government grant of ₹10,000 (US$120) and a sewing machine from an NGO, which the Department of Women and Child Development (WCD) committed to providing. Afroz's family had ostracized him after the crime, but after his release, he was reported to be working as a cook. Five days after Jyoti's death on 29 December 2012, on 3 January 2013, the police filed charges against five adult men for rape, murder, kidnapping, destruction of evidence, and attempted murder of the woman's male companion. Senior lawyer Dayan Krishnan was appointed as the special public prosecutor. Mukesh Singh, Vinay Sharma, Akshay Thakur, and Pawan Gupta denied the charges; some had previously confessed, but their lawyers claimed the confessions were coerced through torture. On 10 January, one of their lawyers, Manohar Lal Sharma, stated in a media interview that the victims were responsible for the assault because they should not have used public transportation or been out at night as an unmarried couple, and that the male victim was "wholly responsible" for failing to protect the woman. The Delhi police filed a charge sheet against the defendants on 13 March 2013 in connection with the robbery of Ramadhir. The four surviving adult defendants were tried in a fast-track court, where the prosecution presented evidence including witness statements, the victim's statement, fingerprints, DNA testing, and dental modelling, completing its case on 8 July. On 10 September 2013, the four adult defendants were found guilty of rape, murder, unnatural offences, and destruction of evidence. They faced the death penalty, and demonstrators outside the courthouse called for their hanging; the victim's father also demanded they be hanged, stating, "We will get complete closure only if all the accused are wiped off from the face of the earth." Lawyers for three of the four stated they would appeal the verdict. On 13 September 2013, the four men were sentenced to death by hanging. Judge Yogesh Khanna rejected pleas for a lesser sentence, stating the case had "shocked the collective conscience of India" and that "courts cannot turn a blind eye to such crimes." The victim's family was present, and her mother expressed satisfaction, saying, "We were waiting with bated breath, now we are relieved. I thank the people of my country and the media." After the verdict, people outside the courtroom applauded. Upon hearing he would be executed, Vinay Sharma collapsed and pleaded with the judge, saying, "Please sir, please sir," and as they left, they shouted, "Brothers, save us!" While on death row, Mukesh Singh blamed Jyoti for being raped, claiming a decent girl would not roam at night and that she was more responsible than a boy, and that she should have remained silent during the assault to avoid being killed. On 13 March 2014, the Delhi High Court confirmed the guilt of each defendant and upheld the death sentences, noting the crime fell into the "rarest of the rare" category allowing capital punishment. The lawyers of the four men filed appeals to the Supreme Court. On 15 March 2014, the Supreme Court stayed the execution of Mukesh Singh and Pawan Gupta to allow appeals on 31 March, later extending the stay to the second week of July. On 2 June, Sharma and Thakur also requested a stay to appeal their convictions, and on 14 July, their execution was stayed. On 27 August 2015, Vinay, Akshay, Mukesh, and Pawan were convicted of robbing Ramadhir and sentenced to 10 years' imprisonment. On 5 May 2017, the Supreme Court rejected the convicts' appeal, upholding the death sentence, stating they had committed a "barbaric crime" that had "shaken society's conscience," and the verdict was well received by the victim's family and civil society. Legal experts noted the convicts still had the right to file a review petition. On 9 July 2018, the Supreme Court rejected a review petition by three of the convicts. In November 2019, the Supreme Court dismissed a review petition from Akshay, retaining the death sentence, and his lawyer requested three weeks to appeal to the President. In January 2020, a five-judge bench rejected the curative petitions of Vinay Sharma and Mukesh. On 7 January 2020, a Delhi court issued a death warrant for the Nirbhaya rapists, setting the execution date for 22 January 2020 at 7:00 a.m. IST in Tihar Jail. Government authorities and the victim's mother alleged the convicts were intentionally delaying the legal process by filing appeals in stages to postpone execution. Under prison rules, if one convict petitions for mercy, the execution of all others in the case is postponed until a decision is made. Mukesh Singh filed a mercy plea in January 2020. The Delhi government recommended rejection and forwarded it to the Lieutenant Governor. On 17 January 2020, the President rejected the plea, with both the Delhi government and the home ministry recommending rejection. Hours after the rejection, Judge Dharmender Rana issued a second death warrant for execution on 1 February 2020 at 6:00 a.m., following a mandatory fourteen-day reprieve. During the hearing, the court also rejected Mukesh's plea to postpone execution. On 17 February 2020, a third death warrant was issued with an execution date of 3 March 2020 at 6:00 a.m. On 4 March 2020, a fourth death warrant was issued with an execution date of 20 March 2020 at 5:30 a.m. Numerous appeals and petitions were filed by the families and the convicts, including three seeking a stay at the International Court of Justice, but the execution date remained unchanged. On 20 March 2020 at 5:30 a.m. IST, Mukesh Singh, Vinay Sharma, Akshay Thakur, and Pawan Gupta were executed at Tihar Jail. The gallows were specially designed for four people. According to prison officials, the convicts refused a last meal and new clothes, were blindfolded, and did not resist as they were led to the gallows; Vinay Sharma suffered a breakdown and pleaded with the guards. The four were pronounced dead after hanging for 30 minutes. Mukesh Singh reportedly requested to donate his organs. Public protests took place in New Delhi on 21 December 2012 at India Gate and Raisina Hill, the latter being near the Parliament and Rashtrapati Bhavan, with thousands clashing with police and battling Rapid Action Force units. Demonstrators were baton-charged, shot with water cannons and tear gas, and arrested. Similar protests occurred nationwide, including over 600 women in Bangalore, thousands in Kolkata, and online via Facebook and WhatsApp, with users replacing profile images with a black dot. Tens of thousands signed an online petition. Yoga guru Baba Ramdev and former Army chief General Vijay Kumar Singh were among those who clashed with Delhi Police at Jantar Mantar. On 24 December, activist Rajesh Gangwar started a hunger strike, saying, "If my death shakes the system and gets them hanged, I am ready to die," and ended it after 14 days, stating he would continue his fight for stricter rape laws. The Middle Finger Protests, a Chandigarh-based NGO led by Prabhloch Singh, played a key role in the agitations. Seven metro rail stations in New Delhi were closed on 22 December to discourage gatherings at Raisina Hill. On 24 December, police blocked roads to India Gate and Raisina Hill, closed nine metro stations, and imposed a curfew near the presidential residence, citing CrPC section 144. The Hindustan Times accused police of excessive force, reporting 375 tear gas canisters used at India Gate. First Post criticized the government for failing to act positively and using force, lathi-charging, pushing media out, and shutting down metro stations. Police claimed peaceful protests were "hijacked" by hooligans and activists. During one protest, police constable Subhash Tomar collapsed and later died in hospital. Two witnesses claimed he collapsed without being hit, while a third disputed this. Hospital doctors and the post-mortem gave conflicting reports: he died of cardiac arrest, but it is unclear if the heart attack was caused by blunt-force injuries to his chest and neck. Some experts suggest the injuries may have been a side effect of CPR. The Delhi Police arrested eight young men and charged them with Tomar's murder and rioting at India Gate. In March 2013, the police admitted in the Delhi High Court they had no evidence and dropped the murder charges, with the youths calling the move "irresponsible." After Jyoti Singh's death on 29 December 2012, protests were held in Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram, Mumbai, Bhubaneswar, and Visakhapatnam. Many mourners carried candles and wore black dresses; some pasted black cloth over their mouths. The following day, a large number of people protested near Jantar Mantar, with minor clashes and police removal of some protesters. One group observed a one-day hunger strike. All roads to India Gate were closed, and areas where protests had occurred were made inaccessible. Some protesters drew graffiti and slogans condemning the incident and demanding stricter laws and faster justice.

After Jyoti Singh's death on 29 December 2012, widespread protests erupted across India, including in Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram, Mumbai, Bhubaneswar, and Visakhapatnam. Many mourners carried candles and wore black dresses; some pasted black cloth across their mouths. The following day, a large number of people protested near Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, where minor clashes occurred between protesters and police, leading to the removal of some demonstrators. A one-day hunger strike was observed at Jantar Mantar, and all roads leading to India Gate were closed, with areas where protests had gathered previously made off-limits to the public. Protesters spread papers with graffiti and slogans condemning the incident and demanding stricter laws and faster justice. The BJP renewed its call for a special parliament session to discuss the case and adopt stricter laws on crimes against women. New Year's celebrations in Delhi were significantly scaled back, with the Indian armed forces and several clubs and hotels cancelling their parties. The protests also spread across South Asia, with marches and rallies in Nepal, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. In Nepal, hundreds of demonstrators in Kathmandu called for legal reforms and a change in attitudes toward women. In Bangladesh, the human rights group Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) said the Delhi protests had energized demonstrations against sexual violence, noting that men were now participating and that the protests included people from diverse social backgrounds. In Paris, people marched to the Indian embassy, handing over a petition calling for action to make India safer for women. An author for the South Asia Analysis Group described the protests as expressions of middle-class angst stemming from a breakdown of the social contract between the middle class and the liberal state. New Delhi has the highest number of sex crimes among India's major cities, with police data showing an average of one rape reported every 18 hours; reported rape cases increased by nearly 17 percent between 2007 and 2011. Only one of the 706 rape cases filed in Delhi in 2012 resulted in a successful conviction. Between 16 December and 4 January, the Delhi Police recorded 501 calls for harassment and 64 for rape, but only four were followed up with inquiries. The regional program director for U.N. Women South Asia stated that rape cases occur in nearly all cities and rural areas, with victims often dying immediately due to the brutality of the crime, calling the incident a wake-up call. Members of Indian parliament demanded severe punishment for the perpetrators. Sushma Swaraj, then Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, stated that the rapists should be hanged. Sonia Gandhi, Chairperson of the ruling United Progressive Alliance, visited Safdarjang Hospital to meet doctors and obtain updates on the victim’s health. Mayawati, chief of the Bahujan Samaj Party, said proper investigation was needed and that action should be so strict that no one would dare commit such acts again. Jaya Bachchan, an actress and member of the Rajya Sabha, said she was "terribly disturbed" and "ashamed" and felt "helpless" for not being able to act. Meira Kumar, then Speaker of the Lok Sabha, stated that a new law should be introduced and passed to ensure women's safety, emphasizing that existing laws were insufficient and that stricter laws were needed. Delhi’s then Chief Minister, Sheila Dixit, said she lacked the courage to meet the victim and described Delhi as a "rape capital," calling for senior police officials to be held accountable and for the immediate establishment of fast-track courts to handle rape cases swiftly. Three constables who refused to act on Ram Adhar’s robbery complaint were suspended for dereliction of duty. On 24 December 2012, Prime Minister Manmohan Singh issued his first official response, appealing for calm and stressing that violence would serve no purpose. He assured the public that all efforts would be made to ensure women’s safety and expressed empathy, saying as a father of three daughters he felt the incident deeply. He cancelled all official events to celebrate the new year as a tribute to Nirbhaya. Then Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh, Akhilesh Yadav, announced a ₹2 million (US$24,000) financial package and a government job for the victim’s family. President Pranab Mukherjee’s son, Abhijit Mukherjee, argued that the women protesters were not students, comparing the situation to the "Pink Revolution" in Egypt, and claimed he saw many "beautiful women" among them, though he expressed doubt about their student status. The remark was widely condemned as sexist; his sister Sharmistha and their father, the president, disapproved. Maharashtra Chief Minister Prithviraj Chavan also expressed disapproval. Abhijit quickly withdrew and apologised. Spiritual guru Asaram Bapu provoked public criticism by claiming the victim was to blame for her assault, saying she could have stopped it by chanting God’s name and falling at the attackers’ feet. Several celebrities, including Preity Zinta, Shah Rukh Khan, Kareena Kapoor, Amitabh Bachchan, and Farhan Akhtar, expressed outrage on social media, demanding the rapists be castrated or hanged. The incident was featured in the first episode of the second season of Satyamev Jayate, hosted by Aamir Khan, which also addressed other rape cases and the suffering of survivors at the hands of police, medical staff, and the public. The American embassy released a statement on 29 December 2012, offering condolences to Nirbhaya’s family and reaffirming its commitment to ending gender-based violence globally. Nirbhaya was posthumously awarded one of the 2013 International Women of Courage Awards by the US State Department, with the citation stating that her personal ordeal, perseverance in fighting for justice, and her family’s bravery were helping to reduce the stigma and vulnerability that drive violence against women. Indian politician Mulayam Singh Yadav opposed making rape a capital offence, saying "Boys will be boys. Boys commit mistakes." Two years later, in response to his comments and another rape incident in Uttar Pradesh where his party was in power, UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said "We say no to the dismissive, destructive attitude of, 'Boys will be boys'" and stated that violence against women must never be accepted, excused, or tolerated, asserting that every girl and woman has the right to be respected, valued, and protected. UN Women called on the Government of India and the Government of Delhi to take radical reforms, ensure justice, and provide robust public services to make women’s lives safer. In response to Western media criticism of India, Jessica Valenti, writing in The Nation, argued that rape is also common in the United States, but US commentators deny or minimize its systemic nature while attacking India for a supposed rape culture. Activist Eve Ensler, who organized One Billion Rising, said the gang rape and murder was a turning point in India and globally, noting that she had never seen sexual violence break through public consciousness so dramatically, appearing on every newspaper’s front page, in college discussions, and in restaurants, and that India was leading the world in fast-tracking laws, sexual education, and examining patriarchal structures and masculinity. In the aftermath, female tourism to India fell by 35% compared to the previous year, according to an ASSOCHAM industry survey. The UK Foreign Office revised its travel advice and advised women against traveling alone. In 2014, Finance Minister Arun Jaitley stated that one incident of rape in Delhi was enough to cost the country billions in lost tourism. In response to the protests, central and state governments announced measures to improve women’s safety. The Government of Karnataka launched a 24/7 dedicated helpline (1091) operated by state police for sexual abuse complaints and considered setting up fast-track courts for pending cases. The Government of Tamil Nadu announced a 13-point action plan, treating sexual assault as a grave crime, assigning top police officials to probe such cases, and conducting daily hearings in fast-track courts with women prosecutors appointed as government counsels. The Jammu and Kashmir government announced plans to revise state laws on sexual offenses and gender crimes. The Government of Himachal Pradesh established state and district-level committees to review progress in cases of crimes against women. Despite these responses, Singh endured significant hardship during and after the protests, facing a demeaning medical examination, a harsh court cross-examination, salacious media coverage, and an insensitive societal response, including from people who knew her. On 22 December 2012, a judicial committee headed by J. S. Verma, a former Chief Justice of India, was appointed by the central government to submit a report within 30 days suggesting amendments to criminal law to address sexual assault. The committee urged the public, legal professionals, NGOs, and women’s groups to share views on possible legal amendments to ensure quicker investigations, prosecutions, trials, and enhanced punishments for extreme sexual assaults. The committee held its first meeting on 26 December 2012 and received over 6,000 emails with suggestions. The report was submitted after 29 days, having considered 80,000 suggestions, and identified government and police failures as the root cause of crimes against women. It recommended reviewing the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 in conflict zones and setting the maximum punishment for rape as the death penalty, rather than life imprisonment. The committee did not support lowering the age of adulthood from 18 to 16. On 26 December 2012, a Commission of Inquiry headed by former Delhi High Court judge Usha Mehra was established to identify lapses, determine responsibility, and suggest measures to make Delhi and the National Capital Region safer for women. On 1 January 2013, a task force headed by the Union Home Secretary was formed to examine women’s safety in Delhi and review the functioning of the city police. On 3 February 2013, the Criminal Law (Amendment) Ordinance, 2013 was promulgated by then President Pranab Mukherjee, amending the Indian Penal Code, Indian Evidence Act, and Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, on sexual offences. The ordinance introduced the death penalty for rape. According to Minister of Law and Justice Ashwani Kumar, 90 percent of the Verma Committee’s suggestions were incorporated into the ordinance. Critics argue that key recommendations, including the criminalization of marital rape and trying military personnel under criminal law, were ignored. In a December 2013 interview, Nirbhaya’s parents, Badri Nath Singh and Asha Devi, said they were seeking to change the juvenile law in cases like their daughter’s rape and murder. They petitioned the Supreme Court to try the juvenile in a criminal court instead of a Juvenile Justice court. The juvenile defendant, who was just short of 18 years old at the time of the crime, was sent to a borstal youth detention center for three years and then released. In a March 2015 interview with The Tribune, Women and Child Development Minister Maneka Gandhi said the government was moving forward with a law treating juveniles as adults in grave crimes. On 22 December 2015, the Rajya Sabha passed the revised Juvenile Justice Act, proposing that individuals above 16 years of age accused of heinous crimes be treated as adults in court. On 16 December 2013, the first anniversary of the attack, activists held memorials in New Delhi to honor the victim, widely known as Nirbhaya, meaning "fearless." Women’s organizations lit candles and protested against women’s exploitation. University students and others organized a candlelight march at the bus stand in South Delhi where Nirbhaya and her friend Pandey boarded the bus. At a commemorative prayer meeting, political leaders committed to increasing efforts to improve women’s security. Former Chief Minister Sheila Dikshit, speaking with the victim’s mother, said Delhi’s society and authorities would work together to build a permanent legacy for her daughter, promising to fulfill whatever the family desired and to ensure such an incident would never happen again. The parents said they were proud of their daughter’s courage, which they believe inspired more women to speak out. In December 2014, on the second anniversary, the parents remarked that little had changed: "Nothing in India has changed since 16 December 2012. All promises and statements made by our leaders and ministers have turned out to be shallow. Our suffering gives them their moment in the limelight. My daughter asks me what I have done to get her justice. She asks what am I doing so that many more like her get justice and I wake up to realise how helpless and trivial I am..." On 16 December 2015, the third anniversary of the attack, "Nirbhaya Chetna Diwas" was observed with candlelight vigils, prayer meetings, and other events at Jantar Mantar. In a "brave homage to her daughter," Jyoti’s mother, Asha Devi, said, "My daughter's name was Jyoti Singh and I am not ashamed to name her. Those who commit heinous crimes like rape, their heads should hang in shame, not the victims' or their families'." She spoke out against the upcoming release of the juvenile convict and put forth four demands for justice: the juvenile should be sentenced to death, fast-track courts should be established in all courts to offer speedy justice to sexual assault victims, amendments to the Juvenile Justice Act should be passed, and the Nirbhaya Fund should be used to set up high-quality forensic labs.

On 16 December 2015, women's and citizens groups, candlelight vigils, prayer meetings, and other events were held at Jantar Mantar to honor Jyoti on the third anniversary of her death. Jyoti's mother, Asha Devi, described the event as "a brave homage to her daughter" and stated, "My daughter's name was Jyoti Singh and I am not ashamed to name her. Those who commit heinous crimes like rape, their heads should hang in shame, not the victims' or their families'." Devi opposed the upcoming release of the juvenile convict and made four demands for justice: on the third death anniversary of the victim, the release of the juvenile convict is seen as unjust; she does not know if the convict is 16 or 18, but knows he committed a brutal crime and there should be no age limit for punishment; the juvenile convict should be sentenced to death, fast-track courts should be set up in all courts to provide speedy justice to sexual assault victims, amendments to the Juveniles Justice Act should be passed, and the Nirbhaya Fund should be used to establish high-quality forensic labs in all states. The public outrage following the rape and murder sparked hopes for change in India. The government responded by passing new sexual assault laws, including a mandatory minimum sentence of 20 years for gang rape, and creating six new fast-track courts for rape prosecutions. The "Nirbhaya" case was the only conviction among 706 rape cases filed in New Delhi in 2012. Between 16 December 2012 and 4 January 2013, Delhi police recorded 501 harassment allegations and 64 rape cases, but only four inquiries were launched. However, the "Nirbhaya" case increased the willingness of rape or molestation victims to report crimes; police records show that during the final nine months of 2013, nearly twice as many rape victims filed reports and four times as many molestation allegations were made. A National Crime Records Bureau report indicates that 95 percent of cases brought to police were classified as crimes, yet there is a large backlog, with fewer than 15 percent of those charged tried in 2012, leaving 85 percent waiting to come to trial. On 16 December 2013, the first anniversary of the rape was commemorated in London with a public memorial honoring the victim; Meera Syal, whose parents are from New Delhi, spoke about the anger expressed at the time and urged the Indian government to enforce changes from the Criminal Law Amendment Act, which expanded the definition of rape and included new offences such as acid attack, sexual harassment, voyeurism, and stalking. She also emphasized the need for activists to act in solidarity to stop violence against women and girls globally. Following the incident, the government established the Nirbhaya Fund for the empowerment, safety, and security of women and girl children, administered by the Department of Economic Affairs of the finance ministry. However, an Oxfam India report published in 2021 found the fund remains underused and underutilized. Observers note that the victim's ordeal changed public conversations about women's issues, with men joining the discussions; a young woman who participated in the protests said that the taboo on discussing rape and sexual violence had been broken, and that media coverage of sexual violence increased, though she saw no change in rape culture or related brutality, noting that teasing, catcalling, and sexual harassment remain widespread in public and private spaces. She acknowledged that a year is too short to undo centuries of patriarchal norms embedded in homes, institutions, and laws, and that police responsiveness is driven by fear of censure rather than duty. Women in urban India still feel unsafe and often wear clothing that covers their bodies to feel safe. Public officials and commentators frequently claim that women who wear "skimpy" clothing or go out with men "invite" attacks, thus denying it is rape. In reality, most women avoid Western clothing due to fear of sexual assault. The idea that women's attire "provokes assault" is described as victim blaming by government officials, social commentators, men, and even other women. As society and the Indian government have failed to address the root causes, women adopt safety strategies such as ignoring sexual commentary, avoiding eye contact, dressing more modestly, and refraining from going out at night, which has led to women avoiding public spaces, including public transportation, reinforcing the expectation that women should stay at home. Critics argue these avoidance tactics are only temporary fixes to deeper issues of victim-blaming and lack of accountability for men. A 2017 poll by Thomson Reuters Foundation, the first of its kind globally, found Delhi was the fourth most dangerous city in the world for women and the worst in the world for sexual violence, rape, and harassment. In response to the incident, Safecity, a non-profit and free website developed by the Red Dot Foundation and launched in 2012, allows users to make anonymous reports of gender-based harassment, abuse, and violence, and creates publicly available maps of these incidents to raise awareness and advocate for improved public safety. In December 2013, the victim's family and social entrepreneur Sarvesh Kumar Tiwari established the Nirbhaya Trust, an institute to assist women who have experienced violence with shelter and legal aid. Named "Nirbhaya" meaning fearless in Hindi, after the media's name for the victim, due to India's law prohibiting the publication of a rape victim's name, the victim's father stated, "So many people supported us, so... we want [to] help those girls who have no one." Inspired by the protests and international attention, women's rights activists organized the first Women of India Leadership Summit, later renamed the Women of India Summit, in 2013, an annual gathering to develop strategies to empower women, especially in the National Capital Region, so that Delhi is no longer known as the "rape capital of the world." India's Daughter (2015), a documentary directed and produced by Leslee Udwin as part of the BBC's Storyville series, was scheduled for broadcast on International Women's Day, 8 March 2015, on NDTV 24x7 in India and BBC Four in the UK. On 1 March, it was revealed that the filmmakers had interviewed one of the rapists while he was in Tihar jail, which was picked up by Indian media. The Indian government blocked the broadcast in India via a court order on 4 March, and the BBC complied, not broadcasting in India. In the UK, the BBC moved the screening to 4 March and aired it on that date. The film was uploaded to YouTube and went viral on social media; on 5 March, the Indian government directed YouTube to block the video in India, and YouTube complied. The film generated significant controversy in India and worldwide. Because India does not permit the publication of a rape victim's name, the victim was called "Nirbhaya," meaning fearless, due to her efforts to fight off her attackers and her insistence on making a detailed statement to police before her death. However, after her death, the parents were quoted as saying they had no objections to using their daughter's name. In the film, the father stated he was "happy" to reveal her name, Jyoti Singh, and on 5 March said he believed everyone should watch the documentary as it revealed "the bitter truth" about attitudes toward women in India. Still, on 6 March, The Hindu published an article titled "Father objects to revealing gangrape victim's name in 'India's Daughter'" in which the father was quoted as planning legal action over the use of her name. Director and producer Leslee Udwin said the courage and passion of ordinary men and women who protested in unprecedented numbers during the December freeze inspired her to make the film, noting that India led the world in commitment to women's rights. Nirbhaya's father, Badrinath Singh, said the film "holds up a mirror to society" and that its screening signifies the continuation of the struggle his daughter was part of. He stated that since her death, every girl on the street is now like a daughter to him and his wife, and that people need to understand that sons must be taught to respect women. Speaking on 5 March, Singh said: "My wife and I brought up our children with the sole intention of making them good citizens. I can proudly say that we have achieved that. Our daughter has shown society its true face. She has changed the lives of many young girls. She remains an inspiration even after her death. She fought back those devils. We are proud of our daughter." Indian-Canadian filmmaker Deepa Mehta's 2016 film Anatomy of Violence was also based on the incident, exploring the social conditions and lack of mental and sexual education in Indian society that enabled the crime. "A Nation Awakens" is the 296th and 297th special two-part episode of the fourth season of Sony TV's Crime Patrol, originally aired on 21 and 22 September 2013, written by Subramanian S. Iyer and directed by R. Amit Kumar Jha, with principal photography in Mumbai beginning in January 2013, hosted by Anup Soni, and featuring Sanjeev Tyagi as the head police inspector. Richie Mehta, a Canadian filmmaker, created a seven-part web television series titled Delhi Crime in 2019, based on the aftermath and manhunt of the perpetrators, starring Shefali Shah, Rasika Duggal, and Adil Hussain, released on Netflix, and winning Best Drama Series at the 48th International Emmy Awards. The comic book Priya's Shakti was inspired by the Nirbhaya case, with the protagonist fighting against gender-based sexual violence in India and globally. A book on the Nirbhaya case, Courting Injustice: The Nirbhaya Case and its Aftermath, was authored by Rajesh Talwar and published by Hay House in 2013. On 5 September 2014, Bandaru Dattareya, a Member of Parliament and BJP National Vice President, inaugurated "Wo Desh Ki Beti" (Nation's Daughter), a social event in Hyderabad showcasing sixteen poems by Sunil Kumar Verma that depicted the pain of a nation at the gang rape of its daughters. Several artists have created works based on Nirbhaya's story; in January 2014, artists from across India held an art exhibition on Nirbhaya and sexual assault. Contemporary scroll painter Kalam Patua created a painting titled Nirbhaya exhibited at the 8th Asia Pacific Triennial of Contemporary Art. Feminist artist Pritika Chowdhry created artworks reimagining Nirbhaya as a superheroine, including a Nirbhaya superheroine, an Anonymous Nirbhaya mask, and other art projects to advocate against sexual assault. Polish-American artist Monica Weiss created an art memorial for Nirbhaya.
